frontmatter.title: Automated Analytics
frontmatter.subtitle: Second and third interviews: technical, then product.
frontmatter.author: Chris Garlick

blocks.title: Two conversations, two different tests
blocks.intro: You're through the first round. The next two interviews look at different things, so prepare for them differently.

rows: Who
John and Matthew, two Senior Engineers
David (Product Manager) and Joseph (Engineer)
Format
Conversation about how you build software
Talking through a realistic problem together
Covers
Backend, frontend and your own experience
How you approach a problem you haven't seen
Stack
Laravel, React / Angular, AWS
Whatever the problem needs
Not included
No live coding, no take-home test
No single right answer, nothing to prepare
They're looking for
*How you think*, not perfect answers
Good questions, clear reasoning, sensible scope

blocks.title: What both interviews have in common
blocks.body: Both say the same thing in different words: **show your thinking**. They want to hear how you weigh options, what you'd ask, and why you'd choose one approach over another. A confident *"it depends on X, and here's how I'd find out"* beats a guess dressed up as certainty.

items.label: Now confirmed
items.value: The stack is **Laravel, React or Angular, and AWS**. The first guide covered the whole advert; this one goes deeper on those three.

items.label: The product
items.value: AI-driven marketing, recruitment and analysis software: campaign automation and business intelligence for clients.

blocks.title: How to answer a conversation-style interview
blocks.intro: With no code to write, your answers *are* the evidence. Give them a shape.

items.title: Restate or clarify
items.detail: "Just to check, do you mean for a single server or at scale?" Shows you don't rush in.

items.title: Give the default
items.detail: What you'd normally do, in one or two sentences.

items.title: Name the trade-off
items.detail: What it costs, and when you'd choose something else.

items.title: Ground it in experience
items.detail: "On Typeset I..." or "Last time I hit this..." One concrete example beats three general ones.

items.title: Stop
items.detail: Leave room for the follow-up. Senior engineers will dig where they're interested.

rows: "I'd use Redis."
"I'd cache it in Redis with a TTL, because the data changes hourly. If it had to be exact, I'd invalidate on write instead."
"I don't know."
"I haven't used that directly. My guess is X, because Y. I'd check by Z."
A ten-minute monologue
Two minutes, then: "Do you want me to go deeper on any part?"
"We did X."
"*I* did X." They're hiring you, not your last team.

blocks.title: It's fine not to know
blocks.body: They've said they want how you think, not perfect answers. If Angular or a particular AWS service is new to you, say so plainly, then reason about it from what you do know. That *is* the test.

blocks.title: Laravel: how you structure an application
blocks.intro: Expect *"talk us through how you'd build..."* and *"where does this logic live?"*

rows: Request lifecycle
public/index.php → kernel → middleware → router → controller → response, back out through middleware.
Service container
Binds interfaces to implementations; constructor injection; swap a real client for a fake in tests.
Thin controllers
Validate (Form Request), authorise (Policy), call an action or service, return a resource.
Actions / services
One class per business operation, e.g. LaunchCampaign. Reusable from controllers, jobs and commands.
Eloquent
Relationships, scopes, casts. Eager-load with with(); turn on preventLazyLoading() in development.
Queues
Anything slow or external goes on a queue: sends, imports, report builds, AI calls. Jobs must be idempotent.
Events
Decouple side effects: CampaignLaunched → notify, log, sync. Queue the slow listeners.
Testing
Feature tests through HTTP with RefreshDatabase; Queue::fake, Http::fake; unit tests for pure logic.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I keep controllers thin and put each business operation in its own action class. That way the same logic runs from an API call, a queued job or an Artisan command, and it's easy to test on its own."*

blocks.title: Laravel: performance and reliability
blocks.intro: Analytics and automation mean lots of data and lots of background work. Expect a *"this page is slow"* question.

groups.title: "A dashboard page is slow. What do you do?"

items.title: Measure first
items.detail: Telescope, Debugbar or APM: how many queries, how long each, and is it PHP time or database time?

items.title: N+1 queries
items.detail: Hundreds of near-identical queries: eager-load with with() or withCount().

items.title: Slow queries
items.detail: EXPLAIN the worst one; add a composite index matching the WHERE and ORDER BY.

items.title: Too much data
items.detail: Select only needed columns; paginate; aggregate in SQL, not in PHP collections.

items.title: Pre-compute
items.detail: Dashboards read daily summary tables built by a scheduled job, not raw events.

items.title: Cache
items.detail: Cache::remember with a TTL for numbers that don't need to be live; tag by account to invalidate.

rows: Retries
$tries and $backoff; retry transient failures, fail fast on bad data.
Idempotency
updateOrCreate, unique keys, or a processed-message table, so a retry can't double-send.
Big jobs
Split into batches (Bus::batch) or chunk; never load a million rows into memory.
Rate limits
Throttle calls to third-party APIs with RateLimiter or job middleware.
Visibility
Horizon for Redis queues, or CloudWatch for SQS; alert on failed jobs and queue age.

blocks.title: Your own example: memory on a small server
blocks.body: Typeset's production box has under 1 GB of RAM. Large renders were being killed by the kernel (an empty error plus a non-zero exit meant a signal, and dmesg confirmed it). Swap fixed it short term; the proper fixes are fewer concurrent renders and a real timeout. A good story for *"how do you debug production problems"*.

blocks.title: React
blocks.intro: Talk about components, state and data fetching, and the mistakes you know to avoid.

rows: Components
Small, focused, props in and callbacks out. Composition over deep prop drilling.
State
Keep it as local as possible; lift it up when shared; context for app-wide things like the user.
Server state
Data from the API isn't app state: TanStack Query handles caching, refetching and loading states.
Effects
useEffect is for syncing with outside systems, not for deriving values. Clean up and cancel.
Derived values
Compute during render; useMemo only when it's measurably expensive.
Rendering
Re-renders are usually fine; fix real problems with memo, stable callbacks, or splitting state.
Lists
Stable keys from IDs, never the array index for lists that change.
Forms
Controlled inputs, or React Hook Form with a schema (Zod) shared with TypeScript types.
TypeScript
Type props and API responses; unknown for untrusted data, then validate.

blocks.title: Angular, and how it compares
blocks.intro: They use React *or* Angular, so some of the codebase is probably Angular. Know the ideas even if you've used it less.

rows: Building block
Components with a template, class and styles
Function components and JSX
Shared logic
Services, provided through dependency injection
Custom hooks, context
Async data
RxJS Observables; HttpClient returns them
Promises, TanStack Query
Reactivity
Signals (modern) and change detection
useState and re-rendering
Templates
@if, @for, bindings: [prop], (event), [(ngModel)]
JSX with plain JavaScript
Forms
Reactive forms with validators
React Hook Form, Formik
Structure
Opinionated: routing, HTTP, forms, testing built in
A library: you choose the pieces
Language
TypeScript, always
TypeScript by choice

items.label: RxJS in one line
items.value: A stream of values over time. switchMap cancels the previous request when a new one starts, which is ideal for search boxes.

items.label: Unsubscribing
items.value: Use the async pipe or takeUntilDestroyed() so subscriptions don't leak.

items.label: Change detection
items.value: OnPush plus signals means Angular only re-checks components whose inputs or signals changed.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I've worked more with React, but the ideas carry over: components, services instead of hooks, and Observables instead of promises. I'd lean on the team's conventions and get productive quickly."*

blocks.title: Joining Laravel to a React or Angular front end
blocks.intro: The seams between front and back are where real bugs live. Show you've thought about them.

rows: Authentication
Same domain SPA: Sanctum cookie sessions with CSRF. Mobile or third parties: Sanctum or Passport tokens.
CORS
Allow only your front-end origins; credentials only where cookies are used.
Response shape
API Resources for a stable contract; never return raw models with hidden fields leaking.
Validation errors
Laravel returns 422 with field errors; the front end maps them onto the form.
Types
Share a contract: OpenAPI generated from Laravel, then TypeScript types generated from that.
Pagination
Cursor pagination for large or live lists; the front end loads the next page on scroll or click.
Long tasks
Return 202 with a job ID; the front end polls, or listens on a websocket (Reverb, Pusher).
Multi-tenancy
Every query scoped to the client's account, enforced server side, never trusted from the front end.

blocks.title: A common follow-up: "How would you build an export of a big report?"
blocks.body: Don't build it in the request. Queue a job that streams rows to a CSV in S3, mark the export ready, and notify the user with a short-lived signed URL. The page shows *preparing* and then a download link.

blocks.title: AWS for a Laravel application
blocks.intro: Know which service does what and how they fit together. You don't need to be an ops engineer.

rows: Run the app
EC2, ECS on Fargate, Elastic Beanstalk, or Lambda via Vapor / Bref
Containers on Fargate: no servers to patch, scales on load
Database
RDS or Aurora (MySQL / Postgres)
Multi-AZ for failover; read replicas for reporting
Cache, sessions, queues
ElastiCache (Redis)
Shared across app instances; never store sessions on disk
Queues
SQS, with a dead-letter queue
Laravel's SQS driver; workers scale on queue depth
Fan-out
SNS or EventBridge
One event, several consumers
Files
S3, served via CloudFront
Uploads and exports; signed URLs for private files
Email
SES
Bounce and complaint handling matters for campaign sending
Secrets
Secrets Manager or Parameter Store
Not in .env files committed anywhere
Access
IAM roles, least privilege
The app's role can only touch its own bucket and queue
Monitoring
CloudWatch logs, metrics and alarms
Alarm on 5xx rate, queue age, database CPU

groups.title: "Walk us through deploying a Laravel app on AWS"

items.title: Build
items.detail: CI runs tests, builds one Docker image, pushes it to ECR.

items.title: Release
items.detail: Run migrations (backwards compatible), then roll the new image out to ECS behind a load balancer.

items.title: Check
items.detail: Health checks gate traffic; a failed check rolls back to the previous task definition.

items.title: Scale
items.detail: Web tasks scale on CPU or requests; queue workers scale on SQS queue depth.

blocks.title: Stateless web servers
blocks.body: Behind a load balancer any request can hit any server, so sessions, cache and uploads must live in Redis, the database or S3, never on the local disk. A classic follow-up question.

blocks.title: A design question, worked through
blocks.intro: They may ask you to design something on the spot. Here's the shape to follow, using a likely example.

blocks.title: "Clients want a weekly email summarising how their campaigns performed."
blocks.body: A good fit for their product: scheduled, per client, data heavy, and possibly AI-written.

items.title: Who and how many
items.detail: How many clients and campaigns? Which metrics? Their timezone or ours?

items.title: What counts as done
items.detail: Is a plain summary enough at first, or do they want charts and AI commentary?

items.title: Schedule
items.detail: A scheduled command each hour finds accounts whose local Monday 9am has arrived.

items.title: Fan out
items.detail: Dispatch one queued job per account, so one slow client doesn't hold up the rest.

items.title: Build
items.detail: Read last week's numbers from the daily summary tables; render the email; send through SES.

items.title: Record
items.detail: Store a sent_reports row (account, week) with a unique key, so a retry never sends twice.

groups.title: 3. Talk through what could go wrong

items.title: Late data
items.detail: Run after the nightly aggregation finishes, or the numbers will be wrong.

items.title: Failures
items.detail: Retries with backoff; failed jobs alerted; a resend button for support.

items.title: AI commentary
items.detail: Pass the numbers in, ask for structured output, never let it invent figures; cache the result.

items.title: Smallest version
items.detail: Plain numbers first, AI summary as a follow-up, measured by open rate.

blocks.title: Stories to have ready
blocks.intro: *Your own experience* is one of the three things they'll cover. Prepare short, specific stories.

rows: Something you built that you're proud of
**Typeset**: an HTTP API that turns Markdown or JSON into branded PDFs. You designed the schema, built the renderer and front end, and run it in production.
A hard production problem
Renders failing with an empty error on Typeset. You worked out it was the kernel killing the process for memory, fixed it short term, and identified the real fixes.
Learning something new fast
Typeset is written in Rust, and renders with Typst. Neither was your day job.
How you use AI in your work
Claude Code daily: planning, refactoring, writing tests, reviewing. You check what it produces; it speeds you up rather than replacing judgement.
Your Laravel experience
Have two real apps in mind: the problem, how you structured it, one thing you'd do differently.
A disagreement in code review
A time you changed your mind, or changed someone else's, with evidence rather than opinion.
A trade-off you made
Shipping a simpler version first, and what you deliberately left out.

blocks.title: Typeset in one breath
blocks.body: *"It's an API I built that turns Markdown or structured JSON into properly typeset PDFs. It's Rust with Typst for the layout, Postgres and Docker, running on a small DigitalOcean server. I use it for real documents, including the one I prepared for this interview."*

blocks.title: Be honest about scale
blocks.body: If they ask about traffic or team size on your projects, give the real numbers. Then talk about what you'd change at a larger scale. That shows the thinking they're after.

blocks.title: Likely questions, with the gist of an answer

rows: How do you structure a Laravel app as it grows?
Thin controllers, action classes, Form Requests, Policies, API Resources; domain folders once it's big.
How do you find and fix N+1 queries?
preventLazyLoading in dev, Debugbar or Telescope to spot them, with() and withCount() to fix.
When do you reach for a queue?
Anything slow, external or retryable. Keep the request fast; make jobs idempotent.
How do you test a Laravel app?
Mostly feature tests over HTTP; fakes for queues, mail and HTTP; unit tests for tricky logic.
useEffect: what goes wrong?
Missing dependencies, deriving state in effects, no cleanup, race conditions on fetches.
How is Angular different from React?
Framework vs library; DI and services; RxJS; templates vs JSX; signals.
How would you handle a search box?
Debounce, cancel stale requests (AbortController or switchMap), show loading and empty states.
How do you secure an API for many clients?
Auth, then authorisation per record (policies), tenant scoping, validation, rate limits.
How would you deploy and scale on AWS?
Docker image, ECS Fargate behind a load balancer, RDS, ElastiCache, SQS workers scaled on depth.
How do you deploy without downtime?
Backwards-compatible migrations first, rolling deploy, health checks, quick rollback.
What makes code maintainable?
Clear names, small units, tests, consistent conventions, and boring choices where possible.
How do you review someone's PR?
Behaviour and tests first, then design, then style; ask questions rather than issue orders.

blocks.title: Questions to ask John and Matthew
blocks.intro: Engineers enjoy talking about their codebase. Pick three or four.

items: Is the front end React, Angular or both? Is there a plan to settle on one?
How is the Laravel codebase organised: one app, or several services?
What runs on AWS today: containers, Vapor, EC2? What would you change if you started again?
How do you handle the heavy background work: queues, scheduled jobs, data pipelines?
What does testing and code review look like? How often do you deploy?
Where does AI sit in the code: calls to model APIs, your own models, or both?
What's the part of the system you'd most like to rewrite, and why?
What does a new engineer usually find hardest in their first month?

blocks.title: Closing line for the technical interview
blocks.body: *"I enjoyed that. I'm strongest on the Laravel side and comfortable across the stack, and I like the mix of data-heavy backend work and client-facing features you've described."*

blocks.title: What David and Joseph are looking for
blocks.intro: A Product Manager and an Engineer, one realistic problem, and a conversation. It's a simulation of working with them.

rows: Curiosity
You ask about the user and the problem before suggesting a solution.
Product sense
You think about who it's for, why it matters, and how you'd know it worked.
Pragmatism
You suggest a small first version, not the perfect system.
Technical judgement
You can say what's easy, what's hard, and what's risky to build.
Collaboration
You build on their ideas, take hints, and change your mind when they give new information.

blocks.title: Why Joseph is there
blocks.body: An engineer in a product interview is watching for whether you can turn a fuzzy problem into something buildable, and whether you'd be good to work with. Bring the engineering in, but don't jump straight to the database schema.

blocks.title: The most common mistake
blocks.body: Hearing the problem and immediately designing a solution. **Asking questions is encouraged**, so ask them first. The problem as stated is often not the real problem.

blocks.title: A shape for working through any problem
blocks.intro: Not a script to recite. A checklist in your head so you don't skip a step.

items.title: The user
items.detail: Who has this problem? A client's marketing manager, a recruiter, an internal account manager?

items.title: The problem
items.detail: What are they trying to get done? What happens today, and what's painful about it?

items.title: The evidence
items.detail: How do we know? Support tickets, churn, sales calls, usage data?

items.title: Why now
items.detail: What's changed? A big client asking, a competitor, a new capability like AI?

items.title: Outcome
items.detail: What changes for the user and the business if we solve it?

items.title: Measure
items.detail: One or two metrics: adoption, time saved, retention, fewer tickets.

items.title: Several ways
items.detail: Two or three approaches, including a non-software one if it fits.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.detail: Value against effort and risk for each.

items.title: Smallest useful version
items.detail: What can we ship in a week or two that tests the idea with real users?

items.title: Risks
items.detail: What could go wrong: data quality, privacy, cost, performance, trust in AI output.

items.title: Next
items.detail: What we'd learn, and what we'd build next if it works.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"Before I suggest anything, can I ask a few questions about who's running into this and what they do today?"*

blocks.title: Questions worth asking about any problem
blocks.intro: Have these ready. You won't use them all; pick the ones that unlock the problem.

rows: The user
Who exactly? How technical are they? How often do they hit this?
Today
How do they handle it now? A workaround, a spreadsheet, a support ticket?
Size
How many clients does it affect? Is it one loud client or a pattern?
Value
Does it affect revenue, retention or support load? Is anyone paying for it?
Success
If we nailed this, what would we see in three months?
Data
What data do we already have? Is it accurate and timely enough to rely on?
Constraints
Deadline? Team size? Anything we can't change, like a third-party API?
Risk
Personal data involved? Anything clients would be upset to see go wrong?
Scope
What's explicitly *not* part of this?

blocks.title: Listen to the answers
blocks.body: The answers are hints. If David says *"it's mostly our three biggest clients"*, that changes the solution. Say so out loud: *"OK, so this might start as something we do for those three, before building it into the product."*

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.intro: A problem in their world, talked through the way you'd do it in the room.

blocks.title: "Clients say they don't know which of their campaigns are actually working."
blocks.body: Said by David as the opening of the exercise. Below is one way the conversation could go.

items.label: Ask
items.value: Which clients: marketing or recruitment? Do they look at the dashboard now? What do they do with the answer, pause campaigns, move budget? What does *working* mean to them: clicks, applications, hires, sales?

items.label: Suppose
items.value: Recruitment clients, mostly. They see clicks and applications but not which campaigns led to hires. Account managers spend hours building this by hand in spreadsheets.

items.label: Reframe
items.value: The real problem isn't *more data*. It's connecting a campaign to the outcome the client cares about, and saving the account managers' time.

items.label: Options
items.value: A cost-per-hire report by campaign, if hire data exists. Or pull hires from their ATS through an integration. Or an AI summary that highlights the best and worst campaigns each week.

items.label: First step
items.value: Start with the account managers' spreadsheet: build that report for a handful of clients using data we already have. Measure time saved and whether clients act on it.

items.label: Risks
items.value: Hire data may be missing or late; attribution is fuzzy when a candidate saw several campaigns; AI summaries must only state real figures.

items.label: Next
items.value: If clients use it, add the ATS integration to make hire data automatic, then the AI summary on top.

blocks.title: Notice the pattern
blocks.body: Ask, then restate the problem in your own words, then offer options with trade-offs, then pick a small first step and say how you'd measure it. Engineers in the room like hearing *"using data we already have"*.

blocks.title: Scenarios to practise
blocks.intro: Talk each one through out loud for five minutes. These are the kinds of problem they could bring.

rows: Clients want AI to write their campaign copy
Brand voice, approval before sending, measuring if AI copy performs better, cost per generation.
Recruiters get too many applicants to review
Ranking or summarising candidates; bias and fairness; the human makes the decision; GDPR.
A big client is threatening to leave
Find out why first; one client's fix vs a product change; don't build a one-off without a plan.
Dashboards are too slow for large clients
Pre-aggregated tables, caching, loading in stages; which numbers really need to be live?
Support gets lots of *"why is my number different?"* tickets
Timezones, late data, definitions; show *last updated*; explain metrics in the UI.
Clients want to connect their own CRM
Which CRMs most clients use; start with one; webhooks vs polling; what breaks when their API changes.
Campaign emails land in spam
Domain authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), sending reputation, bounce handling, warm-up.
We want clients to log in more often
Why don't they now? Useful alerts and weekly summaries can beat a nicer dashboard.

blocks.text: Ways to prioritise, if they ask

rows: Impact vs effort
Do the high-impact, low-effort things first; question the high-effort ones.
RICE
Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort: a score to compare ideas fairly.
MoSCoW
Must, Should, Could, Won't: useful for cutting scope on a deadline.

blocks.title: Building AI features responsibly
blocks.intro: They're an AI company. Expect AI to come up in the problem, and have a view.

rows: Does it need to be AI?
Sometimes a rule, a filter or a good default does the job more cheaply and reliably.
What happens when it's wrong?
A bad subject line is fine; a wrong figure in a client report isn't. Match checks to the risk.
Is a human in the loop?
Suggestions a user approves are safer than actions taken automatically.
How do we measure quality?
A set of real examples to test against, plus user feedback such as thumbs up and down.
What does it cost?
Cost per call × volume. Cache results, use smaller models where they're good enough.
How fast must it be?
Slow generation belongs in a queue, with the result shown when ready.
Whose data goes in?
Personal data, consent, retention, and what the model provider stores.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I'd use AI where it saves people real time and where a mistake is cheap or easy to catch. For anything with numbers in, I'd have the system calculate them and let the AI only explain them."*

blocks.title: Questions to ask David and Joseph

items: How do you decide what gets built next? Where do ideas come from: clients, data, sales?
How much do engineers shape the product, versus building to a spec?
How do you know if a feature worked after it ships?
Who are your main users day to day: clients' marketing teams, recruiters, your own account managers?
What's the biggest product problem you're working on right now?
How do product and engineering work together week to week?
Where do you see AI taking the product over the next year?

blocks.title: Closing line for the product interview
blocks.body: *"I liked working through that with you. I enjoy the part of engineering where you work out what's really needed before building it, and it sounds like that's how you work here."*

items.title: Rehearse three stories out loud
items.detail: Something you built (Typeset), a hard production problem, a technology you learnt fast.

items.title: Refresh Angular basics
items.detail: Components, services, DI, RxJS and switchMap, signals. Enough to talk sensibly.

items.title: Draw the AWS picture
items.detail: From memory: load balancer, ECS, RDS, ElastiCache, SQS, S3, CloudWatch.

items.title: Practise the design question
items.detail: The weekly report email, out loud, in five minutes.

items.title: Use the product
items.detail: Look at their site and any demo. Who are the users? What would annoy them?

items.title: Practise two scenarios
items.detail: Out loud: ask, reframe, options, first step, measure.

items.title: Have paper ready
items.detail: Note their answers as you go; refer back to them.

items.title: Check your setup
items.detail: Camera, sound, quiet room. No coding, but you may want to sketch.

items.title: Know the names
items.detail: John and Matthew; then David and Joseph. Use them.

items.title: Questions ready
items.detail: Three or four for each interview, from this guide.
